prompt: The client asks: "Should we automate our warehouse?" Fact sheet: automation costs $12M; it cuts labor costs by $3M a year; it cuts the error rate from 2% to 0.5%, saving about $300k a year; our hurdle is a 4-year payback; order volume grows 15% a year; two rival warehouses in the region automated last year. Which is the best recommendation?

options.text: Don't automate. $3M of labor savings pays back in 4 years, right at the hurdle with no margin for error at all.
options.feedback: It leaves out the $300k of error savings, which bring payback to about 3.6 years, and the 15% volume growth.

options.text: Automate. Two rival warehouses in the region did it last year, and we can't fall behind.
options.feedback: What rivals did doesn't make our payback work. $3M of labor savings plus $300k from fewer errors pays back in about 3.6 years, inside our 4-year hurdle.

options.text: Automate the warehouse. $3M of labor savings plus $300k from fewer errors makes the payback about 3.6 years, inside the hurdle.
options.feedback: Right. It leads with the answer and counts both savings.

options.text: Automation pays back close to the 4-year hurdle. Whether to go ahead turns on future volume.
options.feedback: This never commits, even though payback is inside the hurdle and volume is growing.

explanation: Full answer: Automate the warehouse. $3M of labor savings plus about $300k from fewer errors repays the $12M in about 3.6 years, inside the 4-year hurdle, and volume is growing 15% a year. The main risk is that installation disrupts the peak season, so the next step is to schedule it outside peak. What would change the answer: total savings below $3M a year, which would push payback past 4 years.

irrelevant_facts: Two rival warehouses in the region automated last year.
